sm: The episode asks how JD Vance could run for president in 2028 after the Iran war and a heavy Republican midterm loss. Guest Kurt Mills, executive director of The American Conservative, says many younger administration staff hated the war, and that Vance's post blaming Iran for the losses was endorsed by Trump. He argues gas prices decide elections, with the danger zone at seventy to ninety dollars a barrel and oil at one hundred fifteen the day before the midterms. Mills says the country voted for something close to a revolution and that it is open season. He says Israel set the table and Trump ate the meal, so both share blame.

Mills says the American Conservative was founded in 2002 against the Iraq war and was the only administration-connected conservative group to oppose the Iran war. He blames the Washington foreign policy establishment's disconnect from voters on weak leadership, fear and venality. Asked about the administration's reaction, he says it is being demure, that Trump did not fight the results, and that people under fifty-five mostly opposed the war. He calls Ron DeSantis's turn against the war a gold Rolex on the ground, noting his 2024 campaign was surrounded by neoconservatives. He then begins to discuss 2028 Republican options.

Mills says a Republican must be aggressively populist and anti-war to win. He doubts Rubio, Hegseth or Ted Cruz could win a national election, thinks Vance could, and says Tucker Carlson is unlikely to run against his friend Vance. Asked about Democrats who share his foreign policy views, he rejects Medicare for All and a return to early 2020s woke politics, and says Ukraine is to Democrats what Iran is to Republicans. He argues Israel is the biggest issue and that Gaza protests pressured Biden into the early debate, which he thinks cost Biden the election.

The host presses a pro-Israel argument that Israel faces barbaric enemies like Hamas after October 7. Mills grants that October 7 was a horrific invasion and that civilian deaths are a tragedy on both sides. He says a moderate liberal Zionist position could regain ground if Netanyahu loses to Gadi Eisenkot, who opposes regime change in Iran, and cites Rahm Emanuel. He argues Hamas is partly a product of Netanyahu's policies, including allowing Qatari money into Gaza, and that Israel opted against moderate accommodations in favor of paranoia.

Mills says Israel's approach may hasten its collapse and that Netanyahu has undermined the two-state solution for thirty years. On Iran, he says the base case remains a negotiated settlement and that Trump will not use a nuclear weapon, though he could bomb civilian infrastructure. He says an invasion is now unlikely after the election, and that Trump has already committed war crimes by threatening to annihilate Iran's civilization. He argues much opposition to international law is Israel lobby protection. Finally he says a settlement could push oil below ninety dollars; below seventy the party gets reelected, and Harris might have done better with slightly lower prices.
